appraisal_events.evidence: « Je laissai toute fierté vis-à-vis d'Albertine, je lui envoyai un télégramme désespéré lui demandant de revenir à n'importe quelles conditions » ; puis le télégramme de Mme Bontemps, « notre petite Albertine n'est plus », et « Toute ma vie à venir se trouvait arrachée de mon cœur. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage stages the narrator's complete self-abasement — he renounces all pride and begs on any terms — and then his collapse into a new, unknown suffering at the news of Albertine's death, ending in disorientation before Françoise. The dominant local movement is his total emotional and self-possessive defeat.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Car tout le temps j'avais imaginé dans l'absurde ses intentions qui n'avaient été que de revenir auprès de moi et que quelqu'un de désintéressé dans la chose… eussent mieux jugées que moi. » ; lettre : « consentiriez-vous à me reprendre ? … Si c'était que je revienne, je prendrais le train immédiatement. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Albertine's posthumous letters vindicate her: her intentions were simply to come back, and the narrator explicitly concedes that any disinterested observer would have read her better than he did. She is retrospectively elevated in the same stroke that convicts his own suspicious imagination of absurdity.

status_effects.explanation: He surrenders every condition to Albertine, then loses her irrevocably; the passage is governed throughout by grief, dependence, and loss of mental equilibrium.

His interpretive authority is discredited by his own admission that a peace negotiator or a merchant — anyone without imagination — would have judged Albertine's intentions correctly where he did not.
The letters clear her of the motives the narrator had ascribed to her and show her asking humbly to be taken back, so her local standing rises just as she becomes unreachable.

ambiguities: The vindication of Albertine is qualified from within: the narrator notes that she probably wrote both letters at nearly the same moment and antedated the first (« antidater la première »), a small manipulation that could support an ironized reading. The passage nevertheless states plainly that her intentions « n'avaient été que de revenir auprès de moi », so the elevation is read as endorsed rather than ironized.

Françoise's closing conduct is doubly framed — genuine tact and possibly sincere sympathy on one side, an attributed peasant instinct for cruelty and a wish to display « sa clairvoyance » rather than pity on the other — so her local standing does not resolve into a single direction; no event is recorded for her under the two-event limit.
